newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss Christians pray for forgiveness for WW2.
newsitem.headline: Swiss Christians pray for forgiveness for WW2.

text.p: Christian worshippers carried banners condemning anti-Semitism and nuns dressed in white prayed to God to forgive Switzerland for its wartime treatment of Jews in a silent protest in the Swiss capital on Saturday.

Some 5,000 members of Swiss churches and Christian groups gathered in front of the government building in Berne with banners urging quick compensation for Holocaust victims who moved their money into Switzerland for safekeeping.

Switzerland is at the centre of a growing controversy over claims by Jewish groups that its banks are profiting from billions of dollars of unclaimed accounts of victims of the Holocaust, the Nazi drive to eliminate the Jews.
The crisis has fuelled fierce debate about latent anti-Semitism in Swiss society, where shame at having turned back 30,000 refugees trying to escape Hitler -- most of them Jews -- still sits deep.
"We acknowledge our guilt. We ask our authorities to rapidly repair this injustice committed against the Jews," read one banner at the protest.
"Anti-Semitism is deep-seated among our people," lamented another.
The protesters said they were humiliated by Switzerland's treatment of the Jews.
"We ask our Jewish brothers to accept our confessions. We express our regrets," they said a statement.

"We express our vigilance against resurgence of dormant anti-Semitism. In past and contemporary history, actions, words and negligence have caused a lot of grief to the Jewish people and deprived them of their legitimate rights and due respect."

The crisis last month forced the resignation of Switzerland's ambassador to the United States after secret documents in which he called for "waging war" against the Jews were leaked to the press and caused international uproar.
Hopes for a fresh approach grew this week when three biggest Swiss banks created a $70 million Holocaust memorial fund as a good will gesture to show that they take the Jewish charges seriously.
But the banks have not acknowledged any wrongdoing.
New York State has moved to curb business ties by deciding to stop placing short-term deposits in Swiss banks until it is satisfied they had no money of Holocaust victims or their heirs.

New York Banking Superintendent Neil Levin is expected to begin a visit to Switzerland on Monday to review the records of Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) and Credit Suisse Group, two big banks that operated in New York during World War Two.
Levin wants to see if any of the money deposited in New York branches of Swiss banks during the war came from Holocaust dead and as a result were not returned to their rightful heirs.
The Swiss banks say they had already turned over any dormant accounts from the era.
